summary: Defines a method for supporting GMPLS bidirectional label switched paths that have different bandwidth in each direction. It builds on the RSVP model for carrying traffic parameters. This is an experimental protocol, and it was replaced by RFC 6387.

eli5.summary: A two-way road does not have to have equal lanes in both directions. This is a way to reserve more room one way than the other. A later memo replaced it.

subtitle: GMPLS can now support bidirectional label switched paths with different bandwidth in each direction.

tldr.problem: GMPLS originally only supported bidirectional Label Switched Paths (LSPs) where both directions reserved the same bandwidth, but some applications and technologies like Ethernet need different bandwidth in each direction.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three new RSVP objects (UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC, UPSTREAM_TSPEC, UPSTREAM_ADSPEC) that mirror the existing objects but specify traffic parameters for the upstream direction, allowing independent bandwidth reservations.
tldr.outcome: GMPLS can now set up bidirectional paths with asymmetric bandwidth, useful for services like Ethernet. RFC 6387 later superseded this with an improved standard.

today: RFC 5467 is an experimental RFC that was superseded by RFC 6387. The later specification provides a standardized approach to GMPLS asymmetric bandwidth LSPs.

sections.title: Why Asymmetric Bandwidth Matters
sections.content:
GMPLS (Generalized MPLS) is used to set up label switched paths (LSPs) that reserve network resources and forward traffic efficiently across different switching technologies. When bidirectional LSPs were introduced, they could only reserve the same bandwidth in both directions.

However, some networks and technologies need different bandwidth allocations in each direction. For example, a video conferencing link might need more bandwidth for sending video than for receiving audio. Ethernet services in particular benefit from asymmetric bandwidth. This RFC defines extensions to GMPLS so it can establish bidirectional LSPs with different upstream and downstream bandwidth reservations.
sections.eli5: Networks sometimes need more space flowing one way than the other, like a delivery route that sends full trucks in one direction and empty ones back. This explains how to reserve different bandwidth each way.

sections.title: RSVP Bandwidth Model
sections.content:
GMPLS signals LSPs using RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol). Bandwidth information travels in RSVP objects that are opaque to RSVP itself but carry parameters understood by the switching technology. The original RSVP model used SENDER_TSPEC (in Path messages) to describe what the sender generates, ADSPEC (also in Path messages) to report actual resources allocated along the path, and FLOWSPEC (in Resv messages) to specify what resources should be reserved.

When bidirectional LSPs were added, the meaning shifted: SENDER_TSPEC indicated desired resources in both directions, and FLOWSPEC confirmed the allocated resources. However, this model did not separate upstream and downstream bandwidth, making asymmetric LSPs impossible.
sections.eli5: RSVP is a language for describing traffic and reserving network space. Originally it only let one side describe traffic. We need a way for both sides to describe what they send.

sections.title: The Asymmetric Bandwidth Approach
sections.content:
This RFC adds three new RSVP objects that parallel the existing ones but apply only to upstream traffic: UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC, UPSTREAM_TSPEC, and UPSTREAM_ADSPEC. These have RSVP class numbers 120, 121, and 122 respectively, matching the class numbers of the downstream objects (FLOWSPEC 9, SENDER_TSPEC 12, ADSPEC 13).

The approach is generic and works with any GMPLS switching technology. The existing downstream objects are used as before, with the new upstream objects used in the opposite direction. Both the ingress and egress can independently specify their bandwidth needs in each direction, allowing true asymmetric LSP setup.
sections.eli5: Instead of one side describing traffic and the other confirming it, both sides can now describe their own traffic separately. This is simple and works with any kind of switching.

sections.title: The Upstream Parameter Objects
sections.content:
UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC (class 120) must appear in Path messages sent by the ingress and specifies the bandwidth the egress will send upstream. Its format matches FLOWSPEC. UPSTREAM_TSPEC (class 121) appears in Resv messages from the egress and describes the actual upstream traffic flow, with the same format as SENDER_TSPEC. UPSTREAM_ADSPEC (class 122) may appear in Resv messages and reports resources actually allocated for upstream traffic, with the same format as ADSPEC.

The C-Type of each upstream object must match the corresponding downstream object so they use compatible traffic models. When the ingress receives an UPSTREAM_TSPEC that says the egress will send more traffic than the UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC reserved, it can issue a new Path message with an updated UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC to request more resources. If insufficient resources are available, the LSP can be re-routed or torn down.
sections.eli5: UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC says how much bandwidth we reserve for traffic coming back. UPSTREAM_TSPEC describes the traffic the egress actually sends. UPSTREAM_ADSPEC reports how much space was actually available.

sections.title: Packet Format Changes
sections.content:
The RFC specifies new sender and flow descriptor formats for bidirectional asymmetric LSPs. The sender descriptor now includes UPSTREAM_LABEL and UPSTREAM_FLOWSPEC after the downstream objects. The flow descriptor list includes UPSTREAM_TSPEC (and optionally UPSTREAM_ADSPEC) along with the existing FLOWSPEC for each reservation.

Nodes that do not understand these new objects will respond with an "Unknown Object Class" error per [RFC2205], which propagates to the ingress. The ingress can then choose to avoid the incompatible node or terminate the session. This ensures backward compatibility: networks that do not support asymmetric bandwidth can reject these LSPs gracefully.
sections.eli5: The Path and Resv messages grow new fields for upstream bandwidth. Old routers will not understand them and will say so, which is fine.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
This extension reuses and extends RSVP semantics from existing RFCs (2205, 3209, 3473). It does not introduce new signaling messages or change relationships between neighboring routers. All security considerations from RFC 3473 apply; the new upstream objects are protected by the same HIP_SIGNATURE mechanisms as downstream objects.

The extension is limited to Point-to-Point (P2P) LSPs. Support for Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) bidirectional LSPs is not covered and remains for future work. An alternate approach using ADSPEC objects was considered but rejected in favor of this more generic approach. The preferred method works with any switching technology, while the ADSPEC approach was specific to Ethernet.
sections.eli5: This fits with existing RSVP security. It only works for one-to-one paths, not one-to-many. A different way could have worked for Ethernet only, but this way works everywhere.
